# Methods {#sec-data-methods}

## Patient and Public Involvement {#sec-methods-ppi}


## Study design

Our study is based on the TBM study (@jamesTrainBrainMusic2020a), a two-site, longitudinal, randomized, activly-controlled, ("open-label" or unblined) intervention study, in which retired healthy older adults, received prcatical piano training once a week (intervention) or theoretical music lesseons (active control) for 18? (between ... and ...) months to assess cognitive, perceptual-motor, and brain plasticity outcomes. 

piano group, that was activly learning the piano by ... Active control group that was only

Blood samples were taken at three different time points. The first (T0) one week before the weekly cycle of practical or theoretical music lessons were started. The second (T1) after 6 months and the third (T2) again after 6 months so one year after T0.

Because multiple tests were performed on each inidivuals time point (not only blood samples but also fMRI as part of the original study) T0 fell between March and June 2019, T1 between August 2019 and February 2020 and T2 between June 2020 and November 2020.

Auch in meiner Untersuchung? *A small subgroup of participants were recruited as early as in January 2019 (T0), and had their consecutive examinations in August 2019 (T1) and in the end of February/beginning of March 2020 (T2). In other words, their T2 was directly before the lockdown started. Therefore, this small subgroup was excluded from the main analyses*

## Study participants

The participants of the study cohort were recruted at the Geneva Musical Minds Lab, Geneva School of Health Sciences, University of Applied Sciences and Arts Western Switzerland (HES-SO), Geneva, Switzerland and the Hannover Medical School, Dept. for Clinical Psychiatry, Social Psychiatry and Psychotherapy, Division of Clinical Psychology and Sexual Medicine in corporation with the Institut für Musikphysiologie und Musiker-Medizin Hochschule für Musik, Theater und Medien affiliated to the Hochschule für Musik, Theater und Medien Hannover. Possibility for participation was made public through newspaper advertisement and posters in public places. @tbl-demographics summarizes relevant demographic information about the study cohort. Some requirements had been to be met for volunteers to participate in the study. They had to be in overall good health, right-handed, retired and not relying on hearing aids.

## Measurement of DNA methylation

### Target Genes

We focused on the primer regions of three genes commonly neuroplasticity-associated and hypthecised being potentially epigenetically modifiable by playing the piano: BDNF4, PSD95, MAPT (Tau).

### DNA isolation

Genomic DNA (gDNA) was isolated at the Institute of Molecular and Translational Therapeutic Strategies of Hannover Medical School from 50 µL blood using the "NucleoMag Blood 200 µl" kit (MACHEREY-NAGEL GmbH & Co. KG, Düren, Deutschland) in concordance with the instructions of the manufacturer. The isolated gDNA was stored at -20 °C. The blood samples have been received anonymized and prior to gDNA isolation. Then the samples were additionaly randomized *(by doing what?)* to minimize potential batch effects. DNA samples were diluted in 96-well plates to a fixed concentration of 10 ng/µl.

### Bisulfite Conversion

The gDNA of all samples was then bisullfite converted via the "EZ-96 DNA Methylation-Lightning™ MagPrep" kit (Zymo Research Corporation, Irvine, CA, USA) also following the manufacturers instructions.

### Primer design

With Ensembl and Geneious Pro 5.6.7 the primer regions of our target genes were located and the sequences of the primer regions analyzed. Aided by Biocalculator (metabion), NetPrimer (Premier Biosoft), Methyl Primer Express v1.0 (Applied Biosystems) and Bisulfite Primer Seeker (Zymo) we designed primers for PCR with bisulfite-converted DNA (see @tbl-primers-pcr) and sequencing primers (@tbl-primers-seq) - later used to prepare Sanger Sequencing - and orderd these primers from metabion GmbH (Martinsried, Deutschland).

### Gene Amplification

The primers were dissolved in nuclease-free water. The proportions have been predetermined by the manufacturer. The stock solution 100 pmol. It was then used to derive a working solution of 20 pmol (1:5). Both solutions were prexserved atg -20 °C. Amplification was then performed together with HotStarTaq® PCR Master Mix Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Deutschland). The samples were then puriefed with the PCR purification kit "CleanNGS" (CleanNA, Waddinxveen, Niederlande).

### Sanger Sequencing

The purfied PCR prodcus were sequenced with the BigDye Terminator v3.1 Cycle Sequencing Kit (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA) and th e sequencing primers mentioned above (@tbl-primers-seq). The sequencing product were purifed with the "CleanDTR" kit (CleanNA, Waddinxveen, Niederlande).

Then using the Applied Biosystems' 3500 Genetic Analyzer (ABI 3500xL) Capillary electrophoresis was performed.

### Data Processing via ESME

The data derived from the ABI 3500xL was then processed with Epigenetic Sequencing Methylation (ESME) analysis software.

## Numbers analyzed {#sec-results-numbers-analyzed}
1,078 blood samples have been sequenced from the participants for three different genes at three different time points (T0, T1, T2). A decline in the number of samples from T0 to T2 can be seen (@tbl-metadata-sequencing-summary), because not every participant provided blood samples at every time point, because of loss to follow up. This is the reason for the difference between the time points.

Furthermore, not every blood sample could be analyzed successfully (cf. @tbl-metadata-sequencing-summary) due to some qualitative differences in the sequencing process. But in the end, a total of 359 BDNF, 362 Tau and 357 PSD95 samples could be successfully sequenced. This is the reason for the slight difference between genes.

Two further Participants had to be excluded from the analysis, because somehow their methylationvalues for timepoints conflated, so they could not be differentiated anymore.

## Outcomes {#sec-results-outcomes}

### Methylation Level Analysis {#sec-results-methylation-level}

#### Overall and over time {#sec-results-methylation-overall}

Overall the methlation of the three genes was low (Mean \< 0,08, Median \< 0,04). PSD95 had the lowest methylation values.

{{< embed notebooks/eda.qmd#fig-boxplots-genes >}}

#### Per CpG and Gene {#sec-results-methylation-cpg-gene}

Looking at the methlation patterns of every CpG per gene (@fig-boxplots-cpg-all), Tau showed a methylation pattern, that was largely limited to upstream region of the promoter, whereas further downstream CpGs were rarely methylated across individuals. In contrast, for PSD95, CpGs near the end of the promoter region showed notable methylation patterns, while most other sites where mostly none-methylated with little or no inter-individual variability. For BDNF, a comparably localized pattern was less pronounced but further downsstream the CpGs were also less methylated.

{{< embed notebooks/eda.qmd#fig-boxplots-cpg-all >}}

## Principal component analysis (PCA) {#sec-results-pca}

We performed principal component analyses (PCA) separately for each gene, using the correlation matrix. Across genes, the first two principal components explained only a moderate proportion of total variance (BDNF: PC1 28.81%, PC2 16.84%; Tau: PC1 29.02%, PC2 9.22%; PSD95: PC1 17.10%, PC2 11.61%). Accordingly, the scree plots (@fig-scree-all) show only a gradual decrease of explained variance across subsequent components. **(Stimmt nicht für PSD95 und Tau)**

Furthermore, biplots of the first two principal components did not indicate a differing clustering pattern between the two group at any timepoint (@fig-pca-genes). Although the apparent group-wise configuration for PSD95 varied somewhat across time points, this pattern did not amount to a consistent clustering difference.

{{< embed notebooks/PCA/PCA_Covariance_161025.qmd#fig-pca-genes >}}

Noticably, inspecting the loadings revelaed that the variance explained by PC1 was driven primarily by a small fraction of CpGs in every gene (@fig-pc1-loadings). For BDNF, m148, m066, m111 and m058 have been the strongest contributors; for Tau, m331, m337, m310, m315 and m323; and for PSD95: "p95", "p60", "p23". By ranking the absolute PC1 loadings every gene showed an "elbow" pattern (BDNF: between the 4th and 5th CpG; Tau: between the 4th and 5th CpG; PSD95: after the 3rd CpG; @fig-pc1-loadings; see also @tbl-supp-pca-bdnf–@tbl-supp-pca-psd95 for loading ranks).

This concentration of variance is also evident in the methylation distributions across CpGs (@fig-boxplots-cpg-all) already mentioned above (#sec-results-methylation-cpg-gene). These observations motivated stratifying subsequent analyses by considering (i) all CpGs and (ii) only CpGs exhibiting higher inter-individual variability.

{{< embed notebooks/PCA/PCA_Covariance_161025.qmd#fig-pc1-loadings >}}

## Models (LM, GLM, ZIBR) {#sec-results-models}
### Linear Models (LM) {#sec-results-lm}

*Across all mean linear models predicting change scores (T1–T0, T2–T0, T2–T1) for BDNF, Tau, and PSD95, model fit was moderate to high (R² ≈ 0.36–0.74). The baseline biomarker at the earlier timepoint was the dominant predictor in every model, showing a strong negative association with subsequent change (all p < .001). This pattern is consistent with change-score modeling and reflects “room to change” / regression-to-the-mean effects.

In contrast, the group effect (Piano vs Control) was small and not significant in 8 out of 9 models. A single nominal group difference emerged for BDNF T1–T0 (b ≈ −0.011, p ≈ .049), but it was not supported consistently across other contrasts or biomarkers and is likely not robust under multiple-testing control.

Site (Standort), sex, age, and CogTel showed no consistent effects across biomarkers and contrasts.*

### Linear model specification (change-score models)

We modeled biomarker change scores using ordinary least squares regression with baseline adjustment:

$$
Y_{i}^{(b,\Delta)} \;=\; \beta_{0}^{(b,\Delta)}
\;+\; \beta_{1}^{(b,\Delta)}\,\mathrm{Standort}_{i}
\;+\; \beta_{2}^{(b,\Delta)}\,\mathrm{Gruppe}_{i}
\;+\; \beta_{3}^{(b,\Delta)}\,\mathrm{Sex}_{i}
\;+\; \beta_{4}^{(b,\Delta)}\,\mathrm{AgeStart}_{i}
\;+\; \beta_{5}^{(b,\Delta)}\,\mathrm{CogTel}_{i}
\;+\; \beta_{6}^{(b,\Delta)}\,B_{i,t_0}^{(b)}
\;+\; \varepsilon_{i}^{(b,\Delta)},
\qquad
\varepsilon_{i}^{(b,\Delta)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{b,\Delta}^{2}).
$$

The outcome is defined as the change score

$$

Y_{i}^{(b,\Delta)} \;=\; B_{i,t_1}^{(b)} - B_{i,t_0}^{(b)}.
$$

For each contrast $\Delta$, the baseline timepoint $t_0$ is:

$$
t_0 =
\begin{cases}
T0, & \Delta \in \{T1{-}T0,\; T2{-}T0\}\\
T1, & \Delta = T2{-}T1
\end{cases}
\qquad
\text{and}
\qquad
t_1 =
\begin{cases}
T1, & \Delta = T1{-}T0\\
T2, & \Delta \in \{T2{-}T0,\; T2{-}T1\}.
\end{cases}
$$

#### CogTel vs BDNF T1–T0 model correction
*“An automated narrative output initially mis-assigned the coefficient labels for the BDNF T1–T0 model; therefore, coefficients were verified and reported based on the underlying summary(lm) output. The corrected results indicate that baseline BDNF (T0), not CogTel, was the strong predictor of change.”*

#### Limitations
*Results should be interpreted in light of (i) multiple testing across biomarkers and time contrasts, such that isolated nominal p-values near .05 may not be robust; (ii) the use of change-score outcomes together with baseline adjustment, which induces strong negative baseline coefficients and can reflect regression-to-the-mean; and (iii) inconsistent factor coding across some models. Additionally, an automated narrative summary initially mis-assigned coefficient labels in the BDNF T1–T0 model; all coefficients were therefore verified against the underlying model summaries, confirming that baseline BDNF (T0), not CogTel, was the dominant predictor of change.*

### Mixed Effects Models (LMM) {#sec-results-lmm}
#### BDNF
#### Tau
#### PSD95
We fitted a linear mixed model (estimated using REML and nloptwrap optimizer) to predict M_value with Zeitpunkt and Gruppe
(formula: M_value ~ Zeitpunkt * Gruppe). The model included ID as random effect (formula: ~1 | ID). The model's total
explanatory power is weak (conditional R2 = 0.09) and the part related to the fixed effects alone (marginal R2) is of
0.07. The model's intercept, corresponding to Zeitpunkt = T0 and Gruppe = Controll, is at -2.66 (95% CI [-2.94, -2.39],
t(348) = -19.29, p < .001). Within this model:

  - The effect of Zeitpunkt [T1] is statistically significant and positive (beta = 0.59, 95% CI [0.20, 0.99], t(348) = 2.94,
p = 0.003; Std. beta = 0.50, 95% CI [0.17, 0.84])
  - The effect of Zeitpunkt [T2] is statistically significant and positive (beta = 0.95, 95% CI [0.54, 1.37], t(348) = 4.50,
p < .001; Std. beta = 0.81, 95% CI [0.45, 1.16])
  - The effect of Gruppe [Piano] is statistically non-significant and positive (beta = 0.37, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.76], t(348) =
1.91, p = 0.057; Std. beta = 0.32, 95% CI [-8.97e-03, 0.64])
  - The effect of Zeitpunkt [T1] × Gruppe [Piano] is statistically non-significant and negative (beta = -0.51, 95% CI
[-1.06, 0.05], t(348) = -1.80, p = 0.072; Std. beta = -0.43, 95% CI [-0.90, 0.04])
  - The effect of Zeitpunkt [T2] × Gruppe [Piano] is statistically significant and negative (beta = -1.24, 95% CI [-1.84,
-0.65], t(348) = -4.13, p < .001; Std. beta = -1.05, 95% CI [-1.56, -0.55])

Standardized parameters were obtained by fitting the model on a standardized version of the dataset. 95% Confidence
Intervals (CIs) and p-values were computed using a Wald t-distribution approximation.

### Zero-Inflated Beta Regression Models (ZIBR) {#sec-results-zibr}
#### BDNF
#### Tau
#### PSD95
We fitted a logistic mixed model (estimated using ML and nlminb optimizer) to predict prop_adj with Zeitpunkt, Gruppe,
Age_start and Sex (formula: prop_adj ~ Zeitpunkt * Gruppe + Age_start + Sex). The model included ID as random effect
(formula: ~1 | ID). The model's total explanatory power is moderate (conditional R2 = 0.14) and the part related to the
fixed effects alone (marginal R2) is of 0.11. The model's intercept, corresponding to Zeitpunkt = T0, Gruppe = Controll,
Age_start = 0 and Sex = F, is at -1.09 (95% CI [-1.79, -0.38], p = 0.002). Within this model:

  - The effect of Zeitpunkt [T1] is statistically significant and positive (beta = 0.15, 95% CI [0.04, 0.27], p = 0.011)
  - The effect of Zeitpunkt [T2] is statistically significant and positive (beta = 0.26, 95% CI [0.14, 0.38], p < .001)
  - The effect of Gruppe [Piano] is statistically non-significant and positive (beta = 0.09, 95% CI [-0.02, 0.20], p =
0.112)
  - The effect of Age start is statistically non-significant and positive (beta = 1.49e-03, 95% CI [-8.53e-03, 0.01], p =
0.771)
  - The effect of Sex [M] is statistically non-significant and positive (beta = 0.03, 95% CI [-0.04, 0.10], p = 0.419)
  - The effect of Zeitpunkt [T1] × Gruppe [Piano] is statistically non-significant and negative (beta = -0.14, 95% CI
[-0.30, 0.02], p = 0.084)
  - The effect of Zeitpunkt [T2] × Gruppe [Piano] is statistically significant and negative (beta = -0.32, 95% CI [-0.49,
-0.15], p < .001)

Standardized parameters were obtained by fitting the model on a standardized version of the dataset. 95% Confidence
Intervals (CIs) and p-values were computed using a Wald z-distribution approximation.

**Grok: Best model for reporting:
Your original filtered 3 CpGs (p23, p60, p95): Strongest signal, highest biological plausibility (likely regulatory sites), significant interaction.
Or the moderately filtered variable CpGs where interaction survived (previous run with marginal R² 0.001 but p=0.012).

Full dataset as supplementary: Shows effect is CpG-specific, not global (good for discussion: "targeted modulation at dynamic sites").

Reporting Tips

State: "Fixed effects explained ~0.1–2% variance (marginal R²), typical for subtle epigenetic changes at specific promoter CpGs amid high site-specific variation."
Visualize trajectories (emmeans plots)—reviewers love figures over R² numbers.
Compare to literature: PSD-95 methylation changes in interventions are often small but linked to expression/plasticity.**

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

**Hohe Expressionsrate!** aller gene vor allem PSD95 und Tau. The null hypothesis of our study was that playing the piano has no effect on the methylation of neuroplasticity-associated genes like BDNF, PSD95 and Tau. Despite of Tau the null hypothesis could be rejected.
